comment_grading:
Grade Breakdown:
Attendance (Quizzes): 15%
Assignments: 27%
Class Discussion: 3%
Final Exam: 55%
Overall Impression:
The final grade isn’t released, but the grading seems transparent and relatively fair. I ended up with an A+, which was a pleasant surprise. Compared to other cc courses, the assessment design is quite easy if you keep up with the materials.
Attendance / In-Class Quizzes (15%)
Attendance is tracked through 4 in-class quizzes(1 of them is a makeup quiz) based on short supplementary videos shown during the last 30 minutes of some lectures. Each quiz has 4 MCQs (1.5 points each), and you still get 1 point per question even if you answer incorrectly. Only your best 3 quizzes count, which helps boost the score. Most students scored full marks, but the quizzes aren’t purely memory-based—some questions are slightly tricky, so watching the videos carefully is worth your time.
Assignments (27%)
There are two problem sets. The first is very manageable (mean 91.4/100), while the second one takes a bit longer to do (mean 86.1/100) likely due to some trickier parts. The TAs give helpful feedback, and the assignments focus on applying class concepts. Read the full questions carefully before rushing into calculations.
Class Participation (3%)
This is based on how actively you engage—asking or answering questions during or after class. Prof. Ma encourages discussion and is very receptive even to basic or “silly” questions. From what I can tell, each participation counts as 1%, up to a max of 3%. Just speaking up 2–3 times is enough to secure this portion.
Final Exam (55%)
A 3-hour closed-book paper, split into:
35 MCQs (around half the exam)
1 calculation question (~10–15%)
2 short essays (~35–40%)
The MCQs mostly test your understanding of trends and patterns mentioned in class and need you to recall some of detailed points. The essays and calculation questions are straightforward if you've kept up with the course content. Time is not an issue, but you do need to be precise in your answers. Scores aren’t released, but performance on the final seems to weigh heavily on the final grade.

Prof. Ma speaks slowly in his lectures and sometimes use Mandarin Chinese to facilitate his speech, and it may be a little bit difficult to focus on what he intends to talk as he digresses frequently. I agree with the previous comment that you should understand Mandarin Chinese to take this course. However, he is trying hard to use his own experience in explaining the historical incidents that have influenced the demographics in China. For example, he said his name 忠東 means 忠於毛澤東, which was a popular name in the early 1960s. He also recalled the fast on Tian'anmen Square in 1989 before the June 4th incident, where 沒有吃的，但是好多喝的，還有蜂王漿. It is really interesting to listen to these stories.
Prof. Ma will mention what is going to be tested in the exam, so it is useful to follow him during his lectures. The recordings will also be provided, so you can review the lectures before the final exam. Just pay attention that the quality of the recording may not be high enough that sometimes you cannot clearly hear him in the recordings. comment_grading:
Components of Final Grade:
Attendance (in-class quizzes): 15%
Assignments: 27%
Class discussion: 3%
Final examination: 55%
In short: The final grade is not released, but I think the grading is fair (and perhaps better than most other UST courses). I get an A+ in this course, which is much beyond my expectation.
The attendance is recorded by 3 quizzes based on supplementary videos played in the last 30 minutes of some classes. Every quiz contains 4 MCQs with 1.5 points each, and you can get 1 point each even you choose the wrong answer. The final score is calculated by the best 3 out of 4 quizzes, and I think most of the students (including me) get full marks. However, the quizzes are a little bit tricky, so please spend some time on watching the videos during the lectures.
The assignments are composed of 2 problem sets with calculations. The problem sets are not difficult at all, and everyone gets high marks (median 95/100 and 88/100 for the 2 problem sets). The TAs also provide detailed feedback to the assignments. Nevertheless, I strongly recommend you to read thoroughly through the problem sets before doing the calculation parts. My overall score is around the median (99/100, 85/100) due to some careless mistakes in the second problem set.
Class discussion is also encouraged, especially raising questions during the lecture breaks. Each time a student asks or answers a question, Prof. Ma will record their participation number. Even though some students (like me) keep asking silly questions, Prof. Ma will happily answer them. I guess each record accounts for 1% of the total score, while the maximum is 3%. If this is true, I get full marks in this part.
The final examination is a 3-hour closed book exam. There are 35 MCQs (around 49%), 1 calculation problem (around 11%), and 2 short essay problems (around 40%). The scores are not disclosed. The time is fairly enough for the problems, so please write carefully to make sure you get all key points.

A well-structured and beginner-friendly psychology course with light workload and fair grading. Suitable for students looking for an introductory course with relatively low stress.

The workload was way too heavy for a common core course. This workload is almost comparable to the workload of an honors course. We had two classes per week (not the problem), and before each class, there are required readings, usually one to two. Each reading typically has around 15 pages (some has around 30!), almost full of text. And the readings will be tested in the exams. I think you have to spend 1-2 hours before each class to read the required readings.
The professor said that any good social science course requires readings, and that he has tried making them simple. But I also had SOSC 1969 in the same semaster, and that course does not require any readings at all, and it has a better reputation from both myself and ust space. Also, the readings are definitely not simple. The words are hard, the grammar is complex, and for your information, I got 5** in DSE English Reading (I think the readings are harder than the hardest DSE B2 article). This should be an SOSC course, not a LANG course.
Finally, the group/individual project may also take some time to finish.

comment_teaching:
Prof. Arthur is a very friendly and approachable teacher. He is quite understanding of students and is open for inputs to improve upon the course. Despite being a 3 hour lecture, there are always breaks in between, and there are many activities where we get to move around the class and do discussions -helps reduce sleepiness :")
His explanations are easy to understand and he provides many examples related to our daily lives. Sometimes the pace may be a little fast as there are many topics to cover.
Before each lecture we are recommended to do prior reading, however, the professor still does a recap at the beginning of each lecture which pretty much covers most of the reading materials anyways.
If you have struggles about certain topics, its really helpful to book office hours with the professor to discuss the materials further and avoid misunderstandings.
The TA's are mainly passive during lectures, but I believe they actively take note of students' participation. They pretty much grade most if not all our group projects.
comment_grading:
I believe the most important grade is the midterm, followed by reflection and poster presentation, then the rest of the group projects.
The SD for all group project work is very narrow so the scores are similar for everyone. However, having a nice group will be beneficial for peer evaluation.
Attendance is not mandatory, however it is crucial for getting a high class participation score. I'd also recommend doing the extra credit work (it's a single essay), especially if you're aiming for a high B to A range.

- Interim Report 2 = 10%
- Poster Presentation = 20%

- Within upper quartile for each grade except interim report 1

Additional Comments:
- We're allowed a written/printed 2-sided A4 cheat sheet for midterms, so there's no need to memorize definitions or scientific terms.
However, the midterms are challenging as it is all essay questions and we are expected to be able to connect many concepts to give comprehensive answers.
- Same thing above also goes for our reflection essay and extra credit work. The more references and interconnectedness of concepts, the better.
*Key takeaway -> focus on understanding, interconnectedness, and broader application of class concepts!

comment_content: I believe it was the most enjoyable course I took this semester. The classes were conducted in various ways, not limited to the classroom. Some classes involved going around the school to measure the flow rate of faucets, others required designing a sustainable product. There was even a class that resembled a simulated United Nations session. Additionally, the teacher arranged for us to play tabletop games developed by an environmental game company for almost an entire class (since each class lasted for 3 hours, it was a lot of fun). From the perspective of the course content, this class covers the basic principles and concepts of sustainability. It encompasses a wide range of topics, and there is a significant amount of PowerPoint content. However, the PowerPoint slides can be treated as a form of popular science material, providing informative content. The class meets once a week, and each PowerPoint presentation consists of approximately 100 pages or so of material.
comment_teaching: The teacher is very willing to answer your questions, and during group discussions, they would come around and help your group resolve any issues you encounter. They are approachable outside of class, and you can genuinely feel that they lead by example, practicing the principles of sustainability. Their way of life feels very minimalist.
comment_grading: Possibly due to the common core curriculum, my grades were pretty good. The class had a large number of students. I performed well on my midterm, and for the group assignments, one was slightly below the mean, while the other was slightly above the mean. Our group project was above the mean but not in the upper quartile. My individual essay was slightly above the mean. In the end, my grade was quite good, falling within the A range.
comment_workload: I think the workload depends on how you perceive each class. Some topics, like playing tabletop games, can be very enjoyable, so you may consider them as something fun rather than a burden. Even if a class lasts for 3 hours straight, you won't see it as a burden. The most challenging part of this course, in my opinion, is the first half of the semester when you have to sit through 3 hours of continuous lectures because the midterm exam covers that material, so it's important to pay attention. Overall, there are approximately 2 group assignments, 1 midterm, an individual essay, creating a poster, and a group project that requires preparation and presentation.
